Relative velocity is a **vector subtraction**, and the order of the subtraction decides
the direction.
**Step 1 — set a sign convention.** Take **north as positive**:
v̄_A = +60 km h⁻¹
v̄_B = +40 km h⁻¹
**Step 2 — apply the definition.** The velocity of B **with respect to** A is
v̄_(B,A) = v̄_B − v̄_A
= 40 − 60
= **−20 km h⁻¹**
**Step 3 — read the sign.** Negative means **south**, so
**20 km h⁻¹ towards the south** ✓
**What this means physically.** To a passenger on the faster train A, the slower train B
appears to **drift backwards** at 20 km h⁻¹ ✓ Both are really going north, but B loses
20 km of ground every hour, and from A that looks like southward motion.
**Why the order matters.** The velocity of A with respect to B is the opposite vector:
v̄_(A,B) = 60 − 40 = **+20 km h⁻¹, north** ✓ From B, the train A pulls ahead northwards.
The two answers are equal and opposite, and reading "B w.r.t. A" correctly is half of
this question.
**Why the speeds subtract here.** They move in the **same** direction ✓ Had B been
heading south, we would have v̄_B = −40 and v̄_(B,A) = −100, that is 100 km h⁻¹ south -
which is where the "100 km/h" distractor comes from, with the direction reversed as well.
**A check with positions.** After one hour, A is 60 km north of the start and B is 40 km
north. B is now **20 km south of A**, having begun level with it ✓ exactly a drift of
20 km h⁻¹ southward.
**Reading the distractors.** **Zero** ✗ would need equal velocities. **20 km/h towards
north** ✗ is v̄_(A,B), the reverse comparison. **100 km/h towards north** ✗ adds the
speeds, which is right only for opposite directions ✓
∴ 20 km/h towards south.

The last two seconds **going up** mirror the first two seconds **coming down** - and the
fall from rest is easy.
**Step 1 — use the symmetry of vertical motion.** With air resistance neglected, the
upward flight is the time-reverse of the downward one ✓ The distance covered in the last
2 s of the ascent equals the distance covered in the **first 2 s of the descent**.
**Step 2 — describe that descent.** The body starts the descent **at rest**, at the
highest point, and falls freely:
s = ut + ½gt²
= 0 + ½g(2)²
= **2g** ✓
**Step 3 — note what it does not depend on.** No initial speed appears in the answer ✓
However fast the body was thrown, the **last** two seconds of its rise are always the
same - the final 2g metres before it stops.
**The direct calculation, to confirm.** Let the body reach the top at time T, so u = gT.
Height at time t: y = ut − ½gt².
at t = T: y = gT² − ½gT² = **½gT²**
at t = T − 2: y = g T(T−2) − ½g(T−2)² = ½g(T² − 4)
difference: ½gT² − ½g(T² − 4) = **2g** ✓ independent of T, as the symmetry argued.
**A numerical instance.** Throw a body up at 50 m s⁻¹ with g = 10 m s⁻²: it rises for
5 s. Its height at t = 3 s is 150 − 45 = **105 m**, and at t = 5 s it is **125 m** ✓ a
gain of 20 m = 2g ✓ Repeat with u = 100 m s⁻¹ and the last two seconds again give 20 m.
**Why the answer is written as "2g".** Numerically 2g = 2 x 9·8 = **19·6 m**, and the
options quote the symbolic form because the question says "numerically equal to" ✓
**The companion result.** The speed two seconds before the top is g(2) = **2g m s⁻¹**,
and the average speed over those two seconds is g, giving a distance of g x 2 = 2g ✓ the
same answer a third way.
**Reading the distractors.** **g** ✗ is the distance in the last **one** second,
½g(1)² x 2... in fact ½g, so neither. **g/2** ✗ is the distance in the last 1 s. **4g** ✗
is the distance in the last **2√2** seconds ✓ The t² dependence means doubling the time
quadruples the distance, so these are all distances over the wrong interval.
∴ 2 g.

Two stages, each handled with its own equation, then added.
**Step 1 — the first 10 s, accelerating from rest.**
s₁ = ut + ½at²
= 0 + ½(10)(10²)
= **500 m**
and the velocity reached is
v = at = (10)(10) = **100 m s⁻¹** - the maximum velocity attained ✓
**Step 2 — the next 10 s, at that constant velocity.**
s₂ = vt
= (100)(10)
= **1000 m**
**Step 3 — add.**
s = 500 + 1000
= **1500 m** ✓
**Why the second stage covers twice as much.** Over the first 10 s the body's **average**
speed was only 50 m s⁻¹ - starting from rest and ending at 100 ✓ Over the second it
travelled at the full 100 m s⁻¹ throughout, so it covered exactly double the distance in
the same time.
**Reading it off a velocity-time graph.** The displacement is the **area** under the
graph:
a triangle, base 10 s and height 100 m s⁻¹: ½(10)(100) = **500 m**
a rectangle, 10 s by 100 m s⁻¹: **1000 m**
total area = **1500 m** ✓ the graph makes the factor of two obvious at a glance.
**A check with the average velocity over the whole 20 s.**
1500/20 = **75 m s⁻¹**
which lies sensibly between 50 and 100, nearer the larger as the longer fast stretch
requires ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **2000 m** ✗ treats the first 10 s as if also at 100 m s⁻¹ -
the commonest slip, forgetting that the body started from rest. **1000 m** ✗ counts only
the second stage. **2500 m** ✗ exceeds even the 2000 m upper bound, which no part of the
motion can reach ✓
**A bound worth noting.** The body never exceeds 100 m s⁻¹, so in 20 s it cannot cover
more than 2000 m ✓ That rules out one option immediately.
∴ 1500 m.
